newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech minister rejects import surcharge idea.
newsitem.headline: Czech minister rejects import surcharge idea.

text.p: Czech Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said on Wednesday that he would not favour an import surcharge as a tool to fix the country's bulging trade deficit.

Speaking at a news conference after a cabinet meeting, Dlouhy said he would instead propose stricter adherence to existing import barriers, including enforcement of quality certification and other requirements.
"I believe that the time has not come for imposing it (an import surcharge)," Dlouhy told reporters, adding that he did not want to be "a witness of adopting any strong measures against imports."
Some analysts have suggested that an import surcharge might be a way to stem a massive inflow of goods which have caused the country's balance of payments to worsen signficantly.

"I rather think that the point is to secure enforcement of the already existing legislation, to clarify what we can do in the areas of certification, various permissions and tariff controls," Dlouhy said.
He added that stricter enforcement of existing controls could have a "partial, not decisive impact" on the overall trade balance.
But Dlouhy also said that if the government wanted to use an import surcharge, it should do it without advance warning.

"It is not a thing to be debated (publicly), it either is imposed or not, because otherwise it only leads to an increase in imports as everybody wants to import fast before it is implemented," he said.

Dlouhy, joining other government and central bank officials, has repeatedly ruled out devaluation of the crown to boost exports and combat a burgeoning current account deficit, but some economists have called for a weaking of the currency.

The government is to debate new measures in two weeks aimed at halting the rapid growth of wages which has exceded productivity growth thus widening the trade and current account deficits, and putting pressure on the state budget.
Details of any proposed government measures have not yet been revealed.
The foreign trade deficit showed a 27.2 billion crown deficit in January and February, up from 16.2 billion deficit in the same period of 1996.
The 1996 current account deficit grew to more than eight percent of gross domestic product, from four percent in 1995.
Forecasts for the 1997 trade deficit range around 210 billion crowns, after last year's 160.3 billion.
